newsitem.title: KENYA: Aid agencies sound alarm bells over eastern Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Aid agencies sound alarm bells over eastern Zaire.

text.p: Aid agencies are sounding alarms over more than 200,000 Rwandan refugees in remote eastern Zaire, warning their health is worsening as the government launches a counter-offensive.

The U.S. agency Refugees International called on Tuesday for Zairean authorities to give immediate and expanded access for aid flights despite being preoccupied with its military campaign in the east.
Following a mission to the area, it also urged authorities to find a better site for some 40,000 refugees at Shabunda and to organise an immediate move before they weakened further.
"Much more urgent and effective emergency assistance measures need to be put into place to enable minimum, life -sustaining assistance to get to the refugees and displaced," it said.
"The situation is so complex and urgent that coordination within the U.N. must be tightened, preferably through the appointment of an emergency field coordinator," it added.
"The world wasn't much interested when hundreds of thousands of refugees were dispersed into the forest. Will it save them, now that many of the 'lost' refugees have been found?" it said.
Refugees International said for three months the refugees and internally displaced had been cut off from regular U.N. supplies of food and water since they fled camps in the east.

"Owing principally to the resultant malnutrition, the health of the refugees is now declining precipitously. Many of the most vulnerable...have already died and many young lives are in the blance," it added.
The U.N. refugee agency is warning of a catastrophe in eastern Zaire because food supplies have been cut by fighting to a trickle and refugee repatriation to Rwanda has almost halted.

Half a million Rwandan Hutus in Tanzania were expelled by troops in December. They followed the return from east Zaire of 600,000 Rwandan Hutus and 60,000 Burundian Hutus after rebels overran their camps.
The U.N. Department of Humanitarian Affairs reported on Monday intensive fighting around Walikale town including bombing raids by aircraft as rebels fought an army counter-offensive.
It said many Walikale residents had reportedly fled to the surrounding area to escape the fighting but the effect of the bombing raids on the forested region near the town was minimal.
The Zairean government says its troops regained Walikale last week but rebels say their forces still control the town.
The U.N. World Food Programme said its first overland consignment of 200 tonnes of food arrived in Kisangani on Monday after a 2,000 km (1,200 miles) by train, truck, barge and ferry.
But it added aid agencies were being denied access from rebel-held Bukavu to Shabunda and access to northern areas from Bukavu was restricted. Insecurity is the other major problem.
Refugees International said reaching the refugees and Zairean displaced at Shabunda was particularly difficult.

It said light, DC-3 type aircraft land on a grass strip, deteriorating even under the light pressure so far, and sacks of food were then loaded on bicycles to a small river where they were transferred to canoes and then reloaded on bicycles.
"Refugees and displaced are surviving by eating manioc leaves. Less than five tonnes of supplies have made it to Shabunda," said the agency, adding another site must be found.
It said cholera was already killing refugees among some 120,000 at Tingi-Tingi and U.N. agencies needed immediate assurances of funding to bring in emergency water equipment.
"Those at Shabunda are in especially poor condition, suffering from malnutrition, exhaustion and malaria," it said.
Refugees International also said there should be a new effort to find other pockets of refugees and help them return.
